papers.title: Robust Decoupled Input Filtering for Internal Model Principle-Based Output Regulation of Polynomial Exogenous Signals
papers.abstract: Internal model principle-based controllers regulate polynomial references and disturbances exactly, but only asymptotically, and their transient input can peak and oscillate, increasingly so as the degree of the exogenous signals grows. A filter placed in series with the plant smooths the command but alters the closed-loop spectrum and can destroy stability. We propose an architecture that keeps the filter outside the loop the regulator stabilizes: the internal model is driven by the error of an ideal, unfiltered copy of the plant, the physical plant receives the filtered command, and an auxiliary plant copy absorbs the mismatch between the two inputs. If the filter satisfies blocking conditions at the origin, any gains that stabilize the unfiltered loop can be combined with any such filter without losing regulation of the true error. Under additive plant uncertainty, we derive a small-gain condition that guarantees robust stability and regulation. On a scalar plant, the proposed controller produces a smoother input and a larger input-delay margin than the unfiltered one, and it maintains regulation under a large loss of actuator effectiveness. On a three-mass chain, its tolerance to unmodeled actuator dynamics and delay stays essentially constant as the regulator is made more aggressive.

papers.title: Compactness-uniqueness method for null controllability
papers.abstract: We develop the compactness--uniqueness method for the null controllability of abstract linear control systems on Banach spaces. Our first main result characterizes the null controllable states for systems that are null controllable up to finite dimensional spaces, and shows that null controllability is then equivalent to the Fattorini--Hautus test. Our second main result gives a dual counterpart of this assumption, an observability inequality with a suitable compact remainder. These results unify and extend several known results, such as those on heat equations with nonlocal terms and on the simultaneous controllability of systems. Finally, for a transport equation with nonlocal terms from population dynamics, we characterize the null controllable states after a sharp time, including in the non-reflexive space $L^1$.

papers.title: A family of alternating projection examples whose Cesàro means fail to converge strongly
papers.abstract: In 1965, Bregman proved that the sequence of iterates of the method of alternating projections applied to two closed convex sets with nonempty intersection in a Hilbert space converges weakly to a point in the intersection. The question whether this convergence may actually fail to be strong was settled in a seminal paper by Hundal in 2004. He provided a counterexample featuring a halfspace and a closed convex cone generated by a certain curve. While largely elementary, the details of Hundal's construction and analysis are quite involved. We revisit this seminal example and present a family of such examples that allows for simpler proofs. Our generating curve combines unit vectors with Gaussian inner products and a height determined by a scalar function. The orbits converge weakly --- but not strongly --- to the origin, while their norms have a positive limit for which we give explicit lower bounds. We also prove that the associated Ces\`aro means behave likewise; in fact, this is generalized to alternating proximal mappings whose composition has a fixed point. Finally, these orbits allow interpretations in the context of projected-gradient, proximal-point, and gradient-descent algorithms.

papers.title: Two-Stage Mixed-Integer Quadratic Programming in Polynomial Time
papers.abstract: Lenstra showed that mixed-integer linear programming can be solved in polynomial time when the number of integer variables is fixed and the number of continuous variables is arbitrary. Mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) can be solved in polynomial time when the total number of variables is fixed. However, since MIQP is NP-hard already without integer variables, the analog of Lenstra's result fails unless P = NP. Hence, polynomial-time algorithms for MIQP with an arbitrary number of continuous variables must exploit additional structure. We study MIQPs with two-stage structure, which underlies Benders decomposition and two-stage stochastic programming. A few linking variables, including all integer variables, are coupled with many blocks of continuous variables that interact only through them, both in the constraints and in the objective. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for MIQP with an arbitrary quadratic objective when the number of linking variables and the block size are fixed, while the number of blocks, and hence the number of variables, is arbitrary. The case with no blocks is MIQP in fixed dimension. None of our assumptions can be dropped. Unless P = NP, the number of linking variables and the block size must both be fixed, the blocks cannot interact or contain integer variables, and large blocks cannot be allowed even if their objective is linear. Unless FPT = W[1], the exponent of the running time must depend on both the number of linking variables and the block size.

papers.title: Splitting and Alternating Minimization Methods for Training Orthogonal Deep Feedforward Networks
papers.abstract: Training deep feedforward networks with weight matrices constrained to layer-wise Stiefel manifolds serves as an effective regularization technique to improve generalization. However, the simultaneous presence of orthogonality constraints and nonsmooth activation functions poses severe theoretical and computational challenges for standard stochastic gradient and Riemannian optimization methods. In this paper, we propose two splitting and alternating-based algorithms to train orthogonal deep feedforward networks (OrthDFNs). By introducing auxiliary variables, we decouple the nested nonsmooth compositions and manifold constraints into a structured equality-constrained optimization problem. To solve this model, we develop OrthALM, an inexact augmented Lagrangian method (ALM) that employs a proximal alternating minimization scheme to solve its subproblems. Crucially, every block coordinate subproblem admits an exact, closed-form solution. We establish a rigorous convergence theory for OrthALM, proving that every accumulation point of the generated sequence is a Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) point of the regularized, reformulated problem. Furthermore, we introduce OrthADMM as a practical, proximal-free variant that executes a single inner alternating sweep per multiplier update to accelerate computation. Extensive numerical experiments show that OrthALM attains lower training error and constraint residuals than OrthADMM in most configurations. OrthADMM achieves competitive test accuracy and the lowest reported runtime in most comparisons with the selected baselines.

papers.title: An Inexact Augmented Lagrangian Method for Semidefinite Complementarity Optimization
papers.abstract: Semidefinite complementarity constraints arise in applications such as inverse semidefinite programming and rank-constrained matrix optimization. We develop a structure-preserving augmented Lagrangian method (SPALM) for mathematical programs with these constraints. The method augments the smooth constraints and retains matrix complementarity in its subproblems. We handle these subproblems by an inexact proximal alternating framework with verifiable descent and stationarity conditions. With vanishing absolute subproblem errors, feasible accumulation points of infinite outer sequences are asymptotically M-stationary. Under AM-regularity, these points are M-stationary. We prove that active-set SDCMPCC-LICQ is sufficient for this regularity. For each AL subproblem, the full stationarity residual converges to zero along infinite accepted inner sequences if the initial sublevel set is bounded, the proximal parameters are bounded above and away from zero, and the block errors vanish. If the block errors are also square-summable, an $O(T^{-1/2})$ best-residual bound holds over $T$ accepted iterations. Huber-Stiefel and fixed-basis procedures generate feasible matrix candidates, whose acceptance is verified by descent tests and computable limiting-normal certificates. For rank-constrained correlation matrix approximation, we construct a lifting that preserves the projected feasible set and global optimal value and satisfies active-set SDCMPCC-LICQ at every feasible point. The stationarity guarantees apply to this lifted model. Finite-budget experiments on this lifting and a single-equality observation-fitting inverse SDP meet the prescribed numerical feasibility and stationarity tests in all 120 runs.

papers.title: Understanding the Asymptotic Transience of Q-Learning via Distributional Expansion
papers.abstract: Q-learning has been empirically observed to exhibit substantial transient error. This transient remains uncaptured by the leading Gaussian limit because the central-limit normalization removes the smaller-scale displacement generated by the initial nonlinear evolution. On the other hand, worst-case finite-sample guarantees, while accounting for transient effects, can obscure the mechanisms responsible for the error on a particular problem instance. We develop a finer asymptotic analysis that gives an asymptotically exact characterization of this transient for a fixed instance. Specifically, for synchronous Q-learning in finite discounted Markov decision processes, we separate the last-iterate error into an optimal-policy temporal-difference (TD) component and a nonnegative displacement caused by maximization. The centered TD component has Gaussian fluctuations at scale $n^{-1/2}$, whereas the maximization transient is of order $n^{-1}$ and converges almost surely, after rescaling by $n$, to a random limit. This limit represents the propagated effect of maximization errors generated before the greedy policy stabilizes. We combine this characterization with an Edgeworth expansion of the TD component to identify the corrections to its Gaussian approximation, separating the effects of initialization, non-Gaussian TD fluctuations, and maximization. The results reveal how transient errors arise for individual Q-learning instances and how their effects persist below the central-limit scale.

papers.title: The optimization landscape of robust high-dimensional mean estimation: stability, moment adaptation, and mirror descent reweighting
papers.abstract: We study efficient robust estimation of a high-dimensional mean under strong contamination when the clean distribution has only $p\ge2$ moments, bounded by $\nu_p$. We give a unified proof of stability for every $p\ge2$ with the optimal dimension-free sub-Gaussian rate, linking the reweighting, trimming and truncation techniques of the outlier and heavy-tailed robust literatures through concentration of counting and truncation processes. Building on stability and spectral signatures, we quantify the optimization landscape over sample weights that remove at most a fraction $\varepsilon_{n,k}=k/n$ of the mass, where the trimming parameter $k$ slightly exceeds the number of outliers. An unobserved convex spectral loss has inexact quadratic growth, with curvature $\frac{1-\varepsilon_{n,k}}{\varepsilon_{n,k}}$, relative to a mean-induced Bregman divergence, and the observable spectral loss supplies a dimension-free, inexact, relatively weakly star-convex subgradient oracle for it. This yields a Lyapunov analysis of mirror descent reweighting for $\varepsilon_{n,k}<\frac13$ that covers Hedge, the projected subgradient method, a new mean-induced mirror descent, and a centered multiplicative weights update. Each method uses one top-eigenvector computation per step and attains the optimal sub-Gaussian rate without knowledge of $(p,\nu_p)$. Mean-induced mirror descent further achieves faster optimization rates and last-iterate guarantees, at the cost of a more expensive projection step in higher dimensions.

papers.title: RPX: Certifying Agent-Generated MILP Reformulations at Scale
papers.abstract: We present RPX, an independent certificate checker for AI-generated reformulations of mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs). RPX verifies that every feasible solution of either the original or the reformulated model can be converted into a feasible solution of the other with no worse objective value. This guarantees equal optimal values and enables solution recovery in the original variables. The checker derives the required checks directly from both models and verifies the certificate using exact arithmetic and reusable reconstruction rules. RPX certifies an agent-generated reformulation for each of the 240 instances in MIPLIB 2017 Benchmark v2. The source models contain up to 27.3 million matrix nonzeros. The median time to decode and check a certificate is 0.312 s, with a 95th percentile of 10.1 s.

papers.title: Frank-Wolfe Theorems for Mixed Integer Quadratic Optimization
papers.abstract: The Frank-Wolfe theorem states that a quadratic function bounded from below on a polyhedron attains its infimum. We study when this remains true in the presence of integer variables, for sets defined by quadratic inequalities. Our main result is a complete classification for sets defined by convex quadratic inequalities with rational coefficients and a rational affine hull, a condition that holds for all full- dimensional sets. One integer variable never destroys attainment: if every rational quadratic objective that is bounded from below attains its infimum over the set, even after adding rational linear constraints, the same holds with one integer variable. In dimension at most 2, integer variables never destroy attainment. In dimension at least 3 and with two or more integer variables, attainment holds for every such objective if and only if the set has bounded curvature, that is, it is bounded except along directions in which all constraints are linear. Without convexity, these results remain valid, except that bounded curvature is no longer necessary. Moreover, integer variables can destroy attainment only if there are at least two of them and at least one continuous variable. The result for one integer variable follows from a lifting theorem, which also extends known results for cubic objectives and convex polynomial constraints. Finally, for convex constraints and rational data, attainment holds when the objective is bounded from above, convex, or quasi-convex over a full-dimensional convex set containing the feasible region.

papers.title: Relative-energy stabilization of an irreversible port-Hamiltonian tubular reactor
papers.abstract: This paper develops a relative-energy control approach for a boundary-controlled irreversible port-Hamiltonian model of a non-isothermal tubular reactor around a spatially nonuniform stationary profile. The starting point is a thermodynamic duality between the entropy-based availability used in earlier reactor control and the relative Hamiltonian induced by the irreversible port-Hamiltonian representation. Under physically interpretable stability conditions---positive heat capacity, positive compressibility and positive compositional susceptibility---the Hamiltonian density is shown to be strictly convex, while the corresponding entropy representation is strictly concave. The resulting relative Hamiltonian decomposes into kinetic, compressive, thermal and mixing contributions and yields an exact relative-energy balance in which irreversible dissipation is separated from profile-dependent terms. This structure leads to a bounded monotone distributed jacket feedback that injects thermal damping without cancelling the nonlinear PDE dynamics. A continuous coercivity condition gives a local a-priori decay estimate for sufficiently regular nonlinear solutions, while a composite energy functional provides an exponential estimate for the linearized closed-loop initial-boundary value problem. Structure-preserving PFEM simulations are used to verify the predicted dissipation mechanisms and constrained profile regulation.

papers.title: Exact Output Steering with Vanishing Controls in Weighted Shift Dynamics
papers.abstract: Exploiting the rich dynamics of wrapped weighted shifts and their residualizations, we characterize exact projected steering with vanishing initial controls. For wrapped shifts, steering is characterized by an expansive cycle multiplier and a residue separating the source and control channels. For residual shifts, a distinct spectral--toral mechanism emerges: steering through selected conjugate planes is equivalent to radial expansion and an arithmetic parity condition on phase resonances, yielding bounded-gap steering times and quantitative control estimates. For structured machine-learning representations built from orbit dictionaries, we derive a two-scale gain condition for steering coefficients while preserving decoded outputs.

papers.title: Subgradient and Stochastic Finite-Difference Methods for Constrained Strongly Quasiconvex Optimization
papers.abstract: We propose a projected subgradient method for solving quasiconvex minimization problems. By employing the Clarke subdifferential, we prove that the sequence generated by the proposed algorithm converges to a solution of the minimization problem when the objective function is locally Lipschitz continuous and strongly quasiconvex in the sense of Polyak, under the same assumptions required for convex functions with the convex subdifferential. Moreover, we derive explicit convergence rate estimates for both the iterates and objective function values. In particular, compared with the corresponding results for nonsmooth, locally Lipschitz, strongly convex optimization, our analysis replaces strong convexity with strong quasiconvexity while preserving the order of the convergence rate, thereby extending the guarantees to a class of possibly nonconvex objective functions. In addition, we investigate a stochastic finite-difference scheme for minimizing a strongly quasiconvex function subject to inequality constraints defined by strongly quasiconvex functions, and establish a convergence rate of order $O(k^{-1/4})$, consistent with known complexity bounds for stochastic zeroth-order methods.

papers.title: On Star Monotone Operators: Theory and Applications
papers.abstract: Introduced by Solodov and Svaiter \cite{SS}, star monotone operators have repeatedly appeared as a sufficient condition ensuring global convergence of first-order algorithms, without requiring full monotonicity. Yet, despite this recurring role, a systematic study of the class itself has been missing from the literature. This paper fills that gap with the first comprehensive treatment of star monotone operators, a class that strictly encompasses monotone and pseudomonotone operators with nonempty zero sets, together with operators that are strongly quasimonotone along rays and satisfy a radial nondegeneracy condition. We develop basic calculus rules, existence and uniqueness results for zeros, global metric subregularity, and precise structural relationships with classical monotonicity notions. We further demonstrate the versatility of star monotonicity through a Clarke subdifferential characterization of nonsmooth star quasiconvexity, applications to Minty and Stampacchia variational inequalities, linear convergence guarantees for subgradient-type methods, and separable operators related to the Debreu--Koopmans problem.

papers.title: Fast Subproblem Solving in Benders Decomposition for Affine Potential-Based Flow Problems with Topology Switching and Scenarios
papers.abstract: Potential-based flow problems arise for a range of practical problems, like the operation of lossless power networks. The distribution of flows through the network is governed by the potential equation, which relates arc flows and node potentials following arc potential functions. We consider a general variant with affine potential functions, topology switching, and scenarios. It can be solved using a Benders decomposition algorithm, with each scenario corresponding to a subproblem. Subproblem solving time can then significantly contribute to overall running time. We present a fast algorithm to obtain Benders optimality and feasibility cuts from fixed master solutions. Problems with affine potential functions are reduced to equivalent problems where every potential function is the identity function. Optimal primal and dual solutions as well as unbounded dual rays are determined by systems of linear equations (SLE), resulting in a constant number of SLEs solved per subproblem. SLEs are solved using LU-factorizations, with the similarity between primal and dual, scenarios, and master solutions exploited by reusing factorizations via low-rank updates to significantly reduce theoretical complexity. We demonstrate the method on security-constrained optimal transmission switching instances, where subproblem solve time reductions of 97.98 percent compared to a standard LP solver are observed.

papers.title: Exact Decisions and Certified Values in $L_\infty$-Norm Computation from State-Space Representations
papers.abstract: Computing the $L_\infty$-norm of a time-invariant linear ordinary differential control system is a routine task in robust control, usually delegated to floating-point routines that perform well on most practical systems. Behind the numerical value, however, lies a discrete decision: whether a pole lies on the imaginary axis, and whether a mode of a realization is actually a pole of the transfer matrix. Floating-point arithmetic can only replace this decision with a tolerance. This paper explains, for a control audience, what reliable symbolic-numeric computation offers for this problem: exact arithmetic where a decision has to be made, and certified enclosures where a value has to be computed. We show how the problem is turned into a small polynomial system directly from state-space data, how this system is solved in practice, and what it costs. A benchmark on the {\tt COMPleib} library and on families of systems with known norms shows that two standard numerical routines err in opposite directions on the imaginary-axis decision, and never on the same system, while the certified method decides it correctly on every instance tested and computes the norm at a cost comparable to that of the numerical routines on most systems. We conclude with practical guidelines for users of numerical tools.

papers.title: Hyperexponential Stabilization of Nonholonomic Systems by Oscillating Controls
papers.abstract: We address the problem of designing time-varying feedback controls that stabilize a given equilibrium of a nonholonomic system at a faster than the exponential rate. We consider systems with an arbitrary degree of nonholonomy and prove a theorem on practical hyperexponential stabilization under a suitable assumption on the parameterized dither signals. The convergence proof is based on a comparison equation with a prescribed power of logarithmic terms. We apply this result to stabilize a model of a car with two off-hooked trailers.

papers.title: Markov Population Potential Game: An Alternative Framework for Markovian Traffic Assignment
papers.abstract: Understanding the equilibrium behavior of large populations of interacting agents in transportation systems is challenging due to the high-dimensional state space and the coupled decision-making among agents. This study proposes the Markov population potential game (MPPG) that integrates Markov games, potential games, and population games as a unified framework for analyzing such interactions. The framework extends the classical Markov potential game to the population level and establishes theoretical conditions on stage rewards and state transitions under which the Markov population game admits a Beckmann-type potential function. Accordingly, every KKT point of the associated optimization problem yields an MPPG equilibrium. We further demonstrate that if only the reward condition holds, each KKT point of the optimization problem corresponds to a support-restricted $\varepsilon$-equilibrium, meaning the Q-values of any two active actions differ by at most $\varepsilon$, thereby significantly extending the applicability of MPPG. We further establish both priori and posteriori upper bounds of $\varepsilon$ to efficiently evaluate the approximation error. Inspired by the equivalent optimization problem, a projected-gradient (PG) policy iteration algorithm is developed. The theoretical bounds and PG algorithm are demonstrated through numerical experiments on a parametric Markov population game.

papers.title: Probabilistically Exact Convexification of Mixed-Integer Quadratic Optimization with Indicators
papers.abstract: We study the convexification of mixed-integer quadratic optimization with indicator variables. The problem remains NP-hard even when the quadratic matrix has bandwidth two, posing a fundamental obstacle to tractable exact convexification. To overcome this challenge in realistic settings, we introduce probabilistically exact (inner) convexification, a framework that relaxes the requirement of exactness for every objective while preserving exact optimality for statistically relevant ones. Our approach is motivated by inference applications, where the objective is determined by a data vector drawn from a distribution and a regularization vector chosen from a prescribed family. Our convexification preserves the exactness of the optimal value with high probability over the data distribution, simultaneously for every regularization vector in this family. We apply this notion to quadratic matrices of any fixed bandwidth. Despite their worst-case NP-hardness, we construct probabilistically exact convexifications that admit exact extended second-order cone formulations of size polynomial in the dimension $n$ and the inverse failure probability $1/\delta$. The required assumptions for their high-probability exactness are surprisingly mild: they accommodate both light-tailed and heavy-tailed data, including distributions without finite mean, as well as arbitrary nonnegative regularization coefficients.

papers.title: Controlling avalanche sizes in the Abelian sandpile model
papers.abstract: The Abelian sandpile model is a classical framework for studying large cascading events, such as those arising in models of forest fires and earthquakes. This work studies the control of such avalanches through the targeted removal of sand grains. We formulate this sequential control problem as an average-cost Markov decision process in which, before each grain addition, a controller may remove a sand grain from a selected vertex. The objective is to balance the long-run expected avalanche size against the cost of intervention. We analyze local intervention policies, which remove grains from a prescribed set of vertices whenever possible, and establish structural results for the recurrent classes and stationary distributions of the induced Markov chains. When the intervention set satisfies a property called topple-freeness, we sharpen these results, derive expressions for the gain and bias functions, and give necessary and sufficient conditions for optimality on general finite graphs. Finally, we apply the general theory to several specific graph classes and obtain a complete characterization of optimal policies on the one-dimensional lattice, the complete graph and the star graph for every value of the intervention cost.

papers.title: Constructing option portfolio
papers.abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of constructing a portfolio composed of a set of financial options. We present a mixed-integer linear program. We apply our approach to index options for the S&P 500.

papers.title: Quadratic Convexification with Two Switching Variables via Extreme Rays
papers.abstract: We consider the convex hull of the quadratic lift $(x,xx^\top,y)$ of the set $\{(x,y) \mid 0 \le x \le y,\ y \in \{0,1\}^n \}$. Descriptions of this convex hull provide convex relaxations for quadratic optimization with switching variables, including problems with indefinite quadratic objectives and constraints. For $n=2$, we completely characterize the extreme rays of the corresponding cone of nonnegative quadratic functions, which consists of two switching rays, six boundary-product rays, discounted affine-square rays, and a parameterized family of discounted rank-two rays. These families generate the cone, so their linearizations give a complete valid-inequality description of the convex hull in the lifted space. The discounted rank-two rays also show that rank-one liftings cannot generate all valid inequalities. Using this classification, we prove a conjecture of Anstreicher and Burer on an exact semidefinite representation of this convex hull.

papers.title: Minimizing Monotone Norms in Fractional Load Balancing
papers.abstract: We devise a fully polynomial time approximation scheme for minimizing a monotone norm $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert$ over a convex set $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d_{\geq 0}$. We study the multi-customer setting, where $X=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ and the solution set $X_i\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d_{\geq 0}$ is given by a linear minimization oracle for each customer $i$. Our algorithm computes, for any given $\varepsilon>0$, a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate solution. With high probability, it uses $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \varepsilon^{-2}(n+d) \right)$ single-customer linear minimization oracle calls and the same number of generalized KL projections to the dual space $Y=\{y\in \mathbb{R}^d_{\geq 0}: \left\lVert y \right\rVert^* \le 1\}$. We assume no prior knowledge on $X$, and our running time depends only on $n$, $d$, and $\varepsilon$. Our result is robust in the sense that it allows for approximate linear minimization oracles and approximate KL projections. We show that the (approximate) KL projection can be performed efficiently for large classes of monotone norms, demonstrating the applicability of our approach. While such a result (with exact projection) is well-known for the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm via multiplicative weight updates and was recently obtained for ordered norms via a smooth norm approximation and a novel randomization, existing techniques do not extend to general monotone norms. In particular, a key feature used in previous proofs was dual price stability, which was derived from a global contraction property of the KL projection to the dual space $Y$. We show that this property does not extend to general monotone norms. Therefore, we use a different price mechanism, based on the well-known mirror descent paradigm, for which a local contraction property holds and guarantees stability.

papers.title: The One-Skeleton of Multilinear Polytopes and Their Standard Relaxations
papers.abstract: Edge-following methods, such as the simplex method, move along edges of a polytope. Their behavior depends on which vertices are adjacent and on the diameter. We study both for the two polytopes of binary polynomial optimization: the multilinear polytope and its standard linear relaxation. For quadratic polynomials, Padberg showed that two integral vertices are adjacent in both polytopes if and only if the variables where they differ induce a connected subgraph. For higher degree, we replace this subgraph by a contracted hypergraph on the same variables, built from the monomials whose constraints tie these variables together. We show that its connectivity decides adjacency in the relaxation but, unlike in the quadratic case, not always in the multilinear polytope. Adjacency is the same in both polytopes exactly when the relaxation has the Trubin property. We investigate when this property holds and characterize it for cubic polynomials. The contracted hypergraph also yields short paths. The diameter of the multilinear polytope is at most the number of variables, and that of the relaxation is linear in the numbers of variables and monomials. Similar linear bounds hold for the number of pivots between bases of the relaxation.

papers.title: Adaptive linear quadratic optimal control for discrete-time stochastic systems
papers.abstract: In this paper, we consider the adaptive linear quadratic optimal control problem for a class of discrete-time stochastic systems, where the system matrix pair $(A,B)$ is unknown and the state weighting matrix $Q$ in the cost function is not necessarily positive semidefinite. Our proposed adaptive optimal control only assumes that the corresponding algebraic Riccati equation has a stabilizing solution, which weakens the standard controllable and observable assumptions used in the literature. To address this problem, we modify a weighted least squares algorithm by incorporating a random regularization method, which ensures the uniform stabilizability of the family of estimated models. Additionally, a diminishing excitation is introduced in the design of the proposed adaptive control to guarantee the strong consistency of the desired components of the estimates. Finally, by leveraging this family of estimates and employing a suitable switching method, we demonstrate that a certainty equivalence control with such a diminishing excitation is an optimal adaptive control.

papers.title: Optimal higher order convergence rates for the MUON optimizer
papers.abstract: Gradient descent optimization methods are the key tools to train deep neural networks in artificial intelligence systems. In practice, one typically employs suitable accelerated gradient descent optimization methods such as the momentum optimizer, the Adam optimizer, or the MUON optimizer proposed by Jordan et al. in 2024. In 1964 Polyak showed that, in a neighborhood of a local minimizer, the momentum optimizer converges with the rate $(\sqrt{\chi}+1)^{-1}(\sqrt{\chi}-1)$, which is strictly faster than the rate $(\chi+1)^{-1}(\chi-1)$ of the standard gradient descent optimizer, where $\chi\in(1,\infty)$ is the condition number (the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue) of the Hessian of the objective function at the local minimizer. Recently, the same faster rate has been established for the Adam optimizer. In this work we show that the MUON optimizer achieves the same higher speed of convergence and we establish the optimality of the obtained convergence rates. More specifically, we propose a precise concept for measuring the speed of convergence of gradient descent optimization methods, and we establish optimal convergence rates for the standard gradient descent, the momentum, the RMSprop, the Adam, and the MUON optimizers.

papers.title: Proximal random reshuffling with inexact gradients for nonconvex composite optimization
papers.abstract: We design and justify a proximal inexact random reshuffling method for minimizing sums of the finite average of functions with Lipschitz continuous gradients and lower semicontinuous regularizers that may be nonconvex. Each epoch visits every component once, using inexact gradients with a prescribed tolerance, and ends with a single proximal step. Our analysis is pathwise: it holds for every sequence of permutations and does not depend on how the reshuffling is performed. We show that when the stepsizes and error tolerances satisfy suitable summability conditions, the objective values converge and every accumulation point is stationary. Furthermore, under the Polyak--{\L}ojasiewicz--Kurdyka condition at a single accumulation point and sufficient decrease of stepsizes, the entire sequence has finite length and converges to that point. For polynomial stepsizes and power-type desingularizing functions, we derive convergence rates for objective values and iterates. Finally, faster objective-value rates are derived when the limit is a local minimizer.

papers.title: Your PID Is Already a Neural Network: Learning Its Gains with Only Three Weights and No Teacher
papers.abstract: A discrete PID controller is exactly a recurrent neural network, a classical state-space fact: a fixed linear memory of the running integral and the last error, read out by three trainable weights that map one-to-one to the PID gains. Networks with bounded hidden states, such as LSTMs of any width, only approximate it. Trained only on a one-step physical cost (the expected cost of one transition from a fixed state distribution), with no demonstrations, teacher controller, or known gains, the network solves a strongly convex least-squares problem, so gradient descent converges from any initialization to the unique one-step optimal PID gains; the limit network is that PID, with the same action on every error sequence. Partitioned regression then shows what extra capacity buys. Orthogonal residual features keep these gains and improve on the PID if and only if they correlate with the part of the optimal action outside the PID span. On a nonlinear second-order example the gap is 5.88% of the optimal PID cost, and 4.00% against PID with a bias; no controller can improve on PID by more on this objective. A residual started at a tuned PID begins exactly at that PID; at the one-step optimal PID, a fixed-feature residual's first gradient step lowers the cost if and only if its features can improve on the PID. Experiments confirm the realization, recovery, and gap results to numerical precision. On held-out plants of three families, under a protocol frozen before the test data existed, a residual warm-started at a heavily tuned PID and trained with it lowers the long-horizon cost by 3.5%, 3.5%, and 1.9%, with family-wise 95% bounds excluding zero, also under distribution shift; a post hoc comparison with the PID tuned alone suggests that most of it comes from the recurrent part in two families. The primary endpoint, a gain of at least 5% from a generic PID start, is not met in any family.

papers.title: An Optimized Expansion Auction Integrating Energy, Flexibility, and Network Constraints
papers.abstract: Auction mechanisms are widely used to support generation investments. In the US, capacity auctions serve as supply-adequacy instruments to address the missing-money problem, whereas in Latin America, energy and capacity auctions procure long-term contracts to support generation expansion. In both settings, accreditation metrics, such as Firm Energy (FE) and Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC), are used to approximate the reliability contribution of selected units and winning projects are selected based on a financial offer. This approach fails to recognize the actual contribution of winners to the multiple services they provide to the system. This limitation becomes more significant with high shares of renewables, as the value of each resource increasingly depends on network and technological constraints, as well as on complementarities within the generation portfolio. Inspired by short-term auctions, such as day-ahead markets, this paper proposes a joint optimization-based auction for generation and transmission investments that internalizes these interactions, capturing the intrinsic value of generation candidates without requiring the computation of FE or ELCC metrics. The auctioneer determines the winning portfolio through an expansion-planning model that explicitly represents network constraints, operational interactions, reliability standards, and multiple scenarios. A case study of the Brazilian system indicates lower system costs, lower risk, and a more diverse portfolio relative to the stylized decoupled procurement approaches currently deployed in many systems.

papers.title: Gradient Flows over Convex Bodies for Learning Optimal Regularizers
papers.abstract: We consider the question of describing gradient flows over the collection of convex bodies. This is motivated by foundational questions arising in inverse problems. Suppose we wish to solve an ill-posed inverse problem using regularization techniques. Can we learn an optimal choice of a convex regularizer directly from prior data? Given a numerical algorithm that computes such an optimal regularizer, is there a principled manner for describing the evolution of its iterates? The objective of this paper is to lay the foundation towards answering these questions. To this end, we consider a criterion of an optimal regularizer based on seeking a convex body that minimizes the expected gauge evaluation with respect to a prior data distribution subject to a volume constraint. The formulation is initially nonconvex, but admits hidden convexity by passing to its polar. We characterize the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions that certify global optimality. We also analyze the $L^2$-gradient flow as well as a minimizing movement scheme with the Hausdorff penalty. Our results show that the objective gap decays exponentially along the gradient flow and we obtain dimension-dependent rates for both the objective gap and distance to the optimal body for the Hausdorff scheme. Finally, we apply the KKT conditions to identify explicit optimal convex bodies. For data where the optimal nonconvex regularizer is the $\ell_p$-quasinorm, $p \in (0,1)$, the optimal convex regularizer is the volume-normalized $\ell_1$-ball. For data described by paired basis atoms, the optimal convex regularizer is the polar of a shifted zonotope.

papers.title: A Polynomial Bound on Split Rank
papers.abstract: We prove that the split rank of a rational pure-integer polyhedron is polynomially bounded in its input length, resolving a conjecture of Basu, Conforti, Di Summa, and Jiang. If the defining system has dense binary encoding length $L$, then $O((L+1)^9)$ split rounds suffice to reach the integer hull in arbitrary dimension.

papers.title: Strategically Robust Multi-Agent Control
papers.abstract: A key source of uncertainty in multi-agent systems is the behavior of other agents. Game-theoretic control approaches ignore this uncertainty, while robust control approaches treat others as fully adversarial. In this paper, we introduce strategically robust multi-agent control to populate the spectrum between these two paradigms. Specifically, in dynamic games, we propose that players are strategically robust and seek protection against misspecified control policies of the other players. This formulation induces a novel equilibrium concept, strategically robust dynamic equilibrium, that interpolates between game-theoretic control and robust control. We study this concept across canonical open- and closed-loop settings and show that accounting for strategic robustness also has computational benefits over classic approaches in game-theoretic control. Numerical experiments on vehicle platooning, inventory management, and network control illustrate resilience to misspecification, and also exhibit a "free-lunch" phenomenon in which strategic robustness can improve performance or social welfare.

papers.title: Discrete Approximation of differential two-stage stochastic linear complementarity problems
papers.abstract: This paper studies differential two-stage stochastic linear complementarity problems, in which an ordinary differential equation (ODE) is coupled with a two-stage stochastic linear complementarity problem (SLCP) under a time-dependent probability distribution. The right-hand side of the ODE involves a solution pair (here-and-now and wait-and-see decisions) of the two-stage SLCP, while the two-stage SLCP involves two functions depending on the time $t$ and the state $x(t)$ of the ODE. Under appropriate conditions, we prove that the solution function of the two-stage SLCP is Lipschitz continuous in $x(t)$ and locally $\frac{1}{2}$-H\"older continuous in $t$, and establish the existence and uniqueness of a classical solution to the differential two-stage SLCP. Moreover, we develop a discrete approximation scheme for the differential two-stage SLCP. We first use a finite-scenario partition with mesh size $\delta_N$ to approximate the distribution, then apply the Euler method for time discretization with step size $h$, and finally solve the resulting finite-dimensional problems using an inexact progressive hedging method with tolerance $\eta$. We prove that the error between a computed solution by the discrete approximation scheme and the classical solution of the original problem is bounded by $C(\delta_N+h+\eta)$, where $C>0$ is a constant independent of $N$, $h$ and $\eta$. Finally, we apply our method to find an equilibrium point of a differential two-stage stochastic two-player zero-sum game. Numerical experiments illustrate the convergence rates and the efficiency of the discrete approximation scheme.

papers.title: To Race or Not to Race? Exploiting Performance Variability in Mixed-Integer Programming via Root-Gated Resource Allocation
papers.abstract: Mixed-integer programming (MIP) solver runtimes vary substantially across random seeds. Parallel replication exploits this variability but can waste computational resources when applied indiscriminately. We investigate whether information from an ordinary solve can guide this allocation decision. We formulate replication under a finite deadline, establish an exact relationship between runtime dispersion and the value of independent searches, and analyze delayed replication and imperfect allocation decisions. Using 101,615 seeded SCIP runs, we examine the association between root-LP dual degeneracy and replication value. We then introduce a non-invasive root-gated policy that preserves the original solver trajectory and launches three additional seeded processes when a root dual-degeneracy indicator reaches a fixed threshold. In a prospective two-hour experiment on 130 paired instances, root-gated racing proves optimality on 77 instances (59.23%), versus 73 (56.15%) for both Single and unconditional Race-4, while reducing active worker-process occupancy by 43.00% relative to unconditional racing. These findings demonstrate the promise of selective parallel resource allocation without solver-source modifications.

papers.title: Optimal One Health control of antimicrobial resistance: a household mean-field model with community feedback and parameters from Burkina Faso
papers.abstract: We study how to combine three One Health interventions against antimicrobial resistance: prescription-only dispensing of antibiotics to people, access to veterinary care for animals, and treatment of household sludge and manure. Each household is a Markov chain on the carriage states of its people, animals and soil, and households are linked through the community, whose prevalence feeds the acquisition rates. We prove that, as the number of households grows, the distribution of household states converges to the solution of a nonlinear mean-field equation. This system is monotone for the stochastic order, so that no intervention increases carriage anywhere, and for every constant intervention it has exactly one equilibrium, which attracts all solutions and is given by a scalar equation. For the optimal control problem we prove existence, necessary conditions, positivity of all controls under a quadratic cost, uniqueness for short horizons, and a turnpike property under an explicit dissipativity condition, which we verify for our parameters by a computer-assisted numerical certification. With parameters from Tenkodogo, Burkina Faso, the optimal combined strategy averts about 17% of human carriage over three years in the baseline scenario, and 11% to 28% over the plausible scenarios for the parameters that the survey cannot identify; these figures are projections conditional on the model. The strategy itself is robust: the value of perfect information on the unmeasured parameters is about 2% of the achievable benefit. A compartmental model with the same transmission rates but without households underestimates the benefit, and targeting the interventions by zone of the town increases it.

papers.title: A Weighted Second-Order Nonlocal Total Variation Regularizer for Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable progress of deep learning in image processing, variational methods remain a fundamental and actively developing framework, offering interpretability, mathematical rigor, and well-founded guarantees. In this work, we introduce a weighted second-order nonlocal total variation regularizer for image restoration, which is based on measuring gradient differences across the image domain and allows for weights that are neither smooth nor symmetric and may vanish outside a search window. We first provide a rigorous definition of the regularizer and prove that it enjoys several desirable properties under realistic assumptions on the underlying weight function. We then consider a nonlocal variant of the variational image restoration model of Chambolle and Lions, and prove the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the associated minimization problem. On the computational side, we develop a discrete formulation of the model and derive the corresponding Chambolle-Pock primal-dual algorithm. Finally, we conduct an extensive experimental evaluation, comparing the proposed regularizer with a range of local and nonlocal, first- and second-order regularizers across several image restoration tasks. The results demonstrate its strong noise-suppression and texture-preservation capabilities, as well as its robustness to nonlocal weights computed under non-ideal conditions.

papers.title: The Query Complexity of Unknown Sparse Gradient Residuals
papers.abstract: We study optimization of an average of \(n\) functions when gradient predictions are exact except for at most \(k\) unknown components. An initial scan may miss these exceptions. For a class of smooth problems, we prove that the optimal worst-case expected number of component-gradient evaluations needed to find an approximate stationary point is \[ \Theta\!\left(\min\left\{nk+\mathcal R,\frac nk\mathcal R\right\}\right), \] where \(\mathcal R\) represents the optimal cost when the exceptional components are known. Prediction evaluations are free. This bound shows that discovering even a few exceptions can cost more than one full scan and can account for most of the gradient evaluations.

papers.title: A Derivative-Free Bellman Equation for Dynamic Time-to-Collision: Two-Sided Certificates and Explicit ReLU Approximation
papers.abstract: Dynamic time-to-collision (TTC) is the first contact time of a prediction flow and defines a feedback map implicitly. We study its capped value function $\VV$ for Carath\'eodory dynamics with bounded, measurable forcing. A self-contained argument establishes local Lipschitz continuity on the transversal collision domain. A derivative-free stopped-step Bellman equation then characterizes $\VV$ uniquely: it advances the prediction for a fixed duration or until contact and adds the elapsed time. A two-sided error bound uses only the candidate's residual along complete stopped trajectories and its error at their endpoints. Exact continuum iteration recovers $\VV$ after finitely many sweeps, including one additional sweep for initializations that violate the boundary condition. We also characterize an optional-duration infimum operator: its fixed points are the dynamic-programming subsolutions, so its residual alone does not identify $\VV$. Finally, on compact subsets of the transversal domain, an optimization-free ReLU construction has explicit size, controlled local residual, and robustness to errors in its nodal TTC values. The optimal velocity model provides the running application.

papers.title: Data-Driven Robust Inventory Planning and Advertising under Product Return
papers.abstract: Online advertising is a central marketing lever for e-commerce retailers, yet it complicates operational planning by simultaneously stimulating product demand and increasing product returns. Motivated by the practice of a fashion retailer on Amazon, we study a retailer's joint inventory and advertising problem across multiple products over a single season, in which advertising has both direct and cross-product spillover effects on demand and returns. Using linear net-demand and return models that capture both effects, we formulate a contextual stochastic optimization model that jointly determines inventory levels and advertising decisions before the selling season. Because ad clicks are realized only after the advertising decision, the predictive covariates are partially observable and decision-dependent, and their joint distribution with the demand and return errors is unknown. We therefore develop an estimate-then-robustify (ETR) approach grounded in a data-driven robust satisficing framework. We establish a finite-sample guarantee on the out-of-sample profit of the ETR solution that holds for any parameter estimator, show that the solution is asymptotically optimal when the estimator is consistent and the profit target approaches the empirical optimal profit, and derive a mixed-integer conic approximation via affine recourse adaptation that is exact for a single product. On the retailer's data, ETR improves out-of-sample profit over conventional estimate-then-optimize by 6.39\% and earns the higher profit in 74.5% of instances, with the largest gains when training data are scarce; the gain falls to 1.02% when the decision model omits cross-product spillovers.

papers.title: Boundary Actuation of a Chain Fountain - Physically Admissible Tracking, Stochastic Limits and Zero-Gravity Circulation
papers.abstract: This paper was inspired by a post on Twitter and by the eight months the author spent at the AASS Centre at Orebro University in 2007. This phenomenon is interesting not only to a physicist, but also to someone like me working in control theory, because of its potential relevance to stabilizing drones and similar flying machines subject to random velocity fluctuations while hovering. A chain fountain can settle without an engineered controller, yet its natural height is selected by transport and boundary forces. We ask how an ideal boundary traction force can sustain a prescribed height or motion. Within an established three-state model, we connect feedback design to force and energy balances and derive sufficient conditions for nominal tracking that preserve the model's mechanical constraints. We also bound the deviations caused by bounded pickup uncertainty. The resulting framework explains how feedback can shape a naturally regulated process and identifies physical limits on the motions it can sustain: stabilizing a mathematical trajectory is useful only if the corresponding motion remains mechanically admissible. This is a preliminary step towards stabilization of the chain in three dimensions.

papers.title: Margin-Inducing Optimal Guidance and Control for Atmospheric Entry
papers.abstract: A method is presented for margin-inducing optimal guidance and control with application to atmospheric entry. The method induces margin in state inequality path constraints during entry while simultaneously retaining a large portion of the non-margin-inducing performance. The margin in the guidance trajectory is based on a differentiable approximation of the maximum of a continuous function. This differentiable approximation is derived from the Kreisselmeier-Steinhauser (KS) function, where the KS function is defined for a function over sampled data. The KS function is first modified into a weighted form where the data points and weights are associated with a multiple-interval Legendre-Gauss-Radau quadrature. This weighted form is then shown to be an approximation of a logarithmic integral. This smooth approximation of the maximum function is then used to formulate a margin-inducing optimal control problem, and this margin-inducing optimal control problem is re-solved at specified guidance update times. The method is applied to a reusable launch vehicle atmospheric entry problem subject to heating rate and dynamic pressure constraints. It is found that the method of this paper produces a guidance trajectory that remains a significant distance from the path constraint limits while maintaining a large portion of the performance of the constrained optimal control problem.

papers.title: On the minimum energy required to trigger a spike
papers.abstract: We formulate and numerically study the problem of finding the minimum energy required to trigger a spike in a three-dimensional conductance-based excitable model. The variational formulation seeks a state trajectory that reaches the boundary of the spiking region with the least \textit{peak} cumulative work supplied through the membrane port. We approximate voltage histories by sums of real exponentials, reducing the problem to a finite-dimensional optimization. The best-found voltage waveform consists of a hyperpolarization phase followed by a depolarization phase, which seems to match the experimentally determined optimal stimulus in squid giant axons.

papers.title: Certified Hierarchical Planning and Tracking: A Learning-Based Approach
papers.abstract: In this paper, we develop a hierarchical control framework for nonlinear dynamical systems with safety constraints. Specifically, a low-fidelity model is introduced for trajectory planning, while a tracking controller is designed for the high-fidelity system. We first characterize the tracking error bound (TEB) using a storage function. Then, we formulate the synthesis of the tracking controller, the storage function, and the TEB as an optimization problem. Following that, we develop an offline learning approach to approximately solve the optimization problem, by incorporating behavior cloning and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solver. We further integrate the learned controller and the TEB into online tracking of the high-fidelity system. This framework enables the control of high-dimensional nonlinear systems with safety guarantees, while maintaining computational efficiency for real-time implementation. Finally, experiments are provided for illustration.

papers.title: Direct Search meets Frank-Wolfe: Inexact Derivative-Free Bilevel Optimization over Polytopes
papers.abstract: In this work we propose BLDS-SIMPLEX, a derivative-free direct search method for the solution of bilevel optimization with polytope constraints at the upper level. The proposed method reformulates the feasible set using barycentric coordinates and explores it using Frank-Wolfe-type directions, relying on a fixed-accuracy black-box oracle for the upper-level objective function. We analyze its convergence properties and complexity in the case of smooth reduced objective; additionally, we analyze a variant for the case of nonsmooth objectives and show its convergence to a specific kind of stationary point that we introduce as a natural generalization to the classic stationarity notions in this setting. Numerical tests on modified instances from BOLIB support the viability of our new approach.

papers.title: Accelerated Transformed Primal Dual Methods for Smooth Convex Optimization Problems with Affine Equality Constraints
papers.abstract: Accelerated transformed primal--dual (ATPD) methods are proposed for smooth convex optimization problems with affine equality constraints. The methods combine primal--dual dynamics with a transformation designed to accelerate convergence. In the strongly convex case, ATPD achieves an accelerated linear convergence rate and matches the known lower bounds on first-order oracle complexity in terms of gradient evaluations and matrix--vector products. The analysis distinguishes these two types of computational work when assessing the complexity of the method. For general convex objectives, a homotopy perturbation strategy is introduced, and an accelerated sublinear rate for the modified Lyapunov energy is proved under a uniform boundedness condition on the primal iterates at all homotopy stages. The acceleration mechanism is based on an exponentially stable ATPD flow and a modified discrete Lyapunov function. This continuous-time perspective guides the construction and analysis of the discrete methods. Numerical experiments on policy evaluation and constrained signal reconstruction problems support the theory and illustrate the efficiency of the proposed methods.

papers.title: Adaptive Constraint Sampling for Stochastic Gradient Methods in Constrained Optimization
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an adaptive constraint-sampling technique for stochastic gradient-based methods to efficiently solve constrained optimization problems with a large number of inequality constraints. The proposed constraint-sampling technique maintains a set of recently violated constraints and draws the constraint used in each iteration uniformly either from this set or from the set of all constraints. This keeps its per-iteration arithmetic overhead independent of the number of constraints. In simulations on synthetic convex optimization problems and in the synthesis of a control barrier function for the Dubins Car, the constraint-sampling technique is shown to significantly outperform uniform constraint sampling.

papers.title: From Metric to Strong Metric Regularity: A Second Subderivative Criterion for Definable Prox-regular Subdifferentials
papers.abstract: We investigate when metric regularity of a subdifferential mapping rules out multiple local inverse branches and therefore upgrades to strong metric regularity. Let $h:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty]$ be proper, lower semicontinuous, definable, prox-regular, and subdifferentially continuous at $(\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{gph}(\partial h)$. We characterize this ``upgrade'' through the second subderivative $q = \mathrm{d}^2h(\bar x|\bar v)$ of $h$. If $\partial h$ is metrically regular, then it is strongly metrically regular if and only if the set of negative curvature directions of $q$ on the unit sphere of $\operatorname{span}(\operatorname{dom}(q))$ has Euler characteristic $0$ or $2$. We also prove a simpler and directly verifiable sufficient condition: nonnegativity of $q$ on the lineality space $\operatorname{dom}(q)\cap(-\operatorname{dom}(q))$ forces a quadratic lower bound for $q$ on its entire domain and hence yields strong metric regularity. In particular, if $\bar x$ is a local minimizer and $\bar v=0$, the second subderivative is nonnegative on its domain $\operatorname{dom}(q)$, which proves a conjecture of Drusvyatskiy, Mordukhovich, and Nghia in the definable setting. The derived principle strengthens this conjecture by replacing local minimality with a weaker second-order condition on the lineality space.

papers.title: Time inconsistent linear quadratic optimal control for mean field games in Hilbert spaces
papers.abstract: This paper studies time-inconsistent linear-quadratic mean-field games governed by stochastic evolution equations in Hilbert spaces. The time inconsistency arises through the dependence of the cost functional on the initial time, while the mean-field interaction enters through the mean of the state distribution. By employing a multiperson differential game approach, we show that the closed-loop equilibrium strategy admits an affine feedback representation characterized by an operator-valued Riccati equation and a novel coupled forward-backward equilibrium system. We establish the existence and uniqueness of mild solutions to the equilibrium system and hence the existence of a closed-loop equilibrium strategy.

papers.title: FanCyqlone: A Parallelized Solver for Multi-Horizon Optimal Control
papers.abstract: Multi-horizon optimal control aims to select optimal control sequences simultaneously for several possible future scenarios, ensuring consistency at the first stage. While this enables advanced model predictive control schemes that explicitly handle prediction uncertainty, solving these problems tends to be costly. We introduce FanCyqlone, a linear solver that exploits parallelism across both time steps and scenario branches. The method builds on Cyqlone to compute the contribution of each branch and combines these results through a shared root problem. We integrate FanCyqlone into QPALM to develop FanCyQPALM, a solver for multi-horizon optimal control problems with general linear stage-wise constraints. We compare its performance with state-of-the-art solvers on spring-mass and quadruped control benchmarks.

papers.title: Conformal Risk Certificates for Portfolio Optimization Under Uncertainty: A Gated Reinforcement-Learning Approach
papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning portfolio policies can optimize allocations from prices, covariances, and prior positions, yet they lack a calibrated, replayable mechanism for certifying that a proposed allocation respects a bounded risk envelope before execution. Regulators increasingly expect automated portfolio systems to provide exactly this kind of pre-trade audit trail, interpretable risk limit, and human-oversight mechanism. Gated Conformal Semantic Risk Control addresses this gap by separating return-seeking allocation from text-conditioned downside-risk verification. An instruction-tuned language model maps timestamped disclosures into schema-validated semantic risk states over macro, liquidity, earnings, and sector channels. These states induce correlated ellipsoidal factor-shock uncertainty sets whose conformal radii are calibrated by rolling finite-sample prediction over localized semantic nonconformity buckets. An asymmetric second-order cone gate then checks each raw PPO proposal against a certified worst-case semantic loss budget. The gate stays inactive for compliant proposals and intervenes only when that budget is exceeded. In walk-forward out-of-sample tests on nine liquid U.S. Select Sector SPDR ETFs, Raw PPO earns a 12.7% annual return while incurring a 4.05% semantic violation rate. Gated-CSRC removes all observed out-of-sample semantic limit breaches while retaining an 11.7% annual return. This 100-basis-point auditable safety premium is smaller than the yield loss imposed by unconditional hard projection, and exact McNemar testing confirms the compliance gain at $p < 10^{-15}$. Loughran-McDonald lexicon controls and time-shuffled text controls fail to reproduce this certificate.

papers.title: Stability of equilibria in discrete-time modified-gradient systems and the multivariate breeder's equation
papers.abstract:
The multivariate breeder's equation $\Delta ar z=G
abla\ln ar W$ is a widely used discrete-time modified-gradient system describing the evolution of continuous traits in organisms. This system could more conventionally be expressed as $x_{k+1}=x_k+P_k
abla f(x_k)$. For its continuous-time counterpart $x'=P(t)
abla f(x)$, it has been proven that an isolated local maximum of $f$ is uniformly stable whenever $P(t)$ is positive semidefinite, as is the case for the "$G$-matrix." Furthermore, the continuous time system is uniformly asymptotically stable when the maximum is an isolated critical point and $\int_0^\infty\lambda_1(P(t))\,dt=\infty$. We show that the literal discrete analog of this result is false: with constant positive definite $P$ the iterates can oscillate or diverge. The result is restored by a single additional hypothesis, a uniform bound on the largest eigenvalue of $P_k$, $\lambda_n$, such that $\lambda_n(P_k)\le 2/L$ where $L$ is a local Lipschitz constant of $
abla f$. Under this bound the maximum is uniformly stable; under a stricter version together with $\sum_k\lambda_1(P_k)=\infty$, the maximum is uniformly asymptotically stable. Given these hypotheses, a level-set estimate of the basin of attraction carries over. Both bounds are sharp, and each remaining hypothesis is shown to be necessary. Biologically, the bound says that genetic variance in every direction must be small relative to the curvature of log mean fitness; outside this regime the mean phenotype can overshoot a fitness peak as hypothesized by Fisher's geometric model. As further application of our results, the same conditions apply to the mean update of Gaussian evolutionary optimization algorithms, in which the covariance of the search population plays the role of $G$.

papers.title: Distributionally Robust BEST-RQ For Speech Representation Learning
papers.abstract: BEST-RQ, based on random projection and quantization, has been a well-established self-supervised learning approach to learn speech representations from large-scale unlabeled audio due to its high performance and efficiency. However, in BEST-RQ representations learned by random quantization can be sensitive to the choice of quantization targets. To address this issue, we propose a distributionally robust extension of BEST-RQ that seeks representations robust across multiple quantization configurations. Specifically, we define groups by codebooks and formulate the training as a group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem. Rather than optimizing solely for the average loss across groups, our approach adaptively reweights groups to emphasize those performing poorly. Additionally, we regularize DRO with a Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent excessive distribution deviation. We evaluate our approach on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset and show that the distributionally robust BEST-RQ achieves superior performance over the conventional uniform average across multiple codebooks.

papers.title: Improved last-iterate bounds for SGD with and without replacement
papers.abstract: In this work, we study last-iterate convergence bounds for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on convex and $\beta$-smooth loss functions and improve the bound from $\cO((\log T)^3/T)$ to $\cO((\log T)^3/(T\log\log T))$ in the interpolation regime. The improvement comes from applying a horizon-dependent multiscale estimate of gradients to the comparison of trajectories. The bound applies to both sampling with replacement and sampling without replacement within one pass.

papers.title: Random feature policy iteration for inverse mean field games with complex geometry and high dimensions
papers.abstract: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free nature and flexibility to handle complex geometries and high-dimensional problems. The method builds on a policy iteration framework for inverse MFGs, which decouples the coupled nonlinear forward-backward PDE system into a sequence of linear PDE and inverse problem solves. The fixed random feature representations preserve this linear structure, allowing the resulting subproblems to be solved by minimizing residuals at sampled collocation points through linear least-squares problems. The mesh-free nature of the method further extends the applicability of the policy iteration framework to inverse MFGs with complex geometry and in high dimensions. Another key advantage is its flexibility in using different spatial approximations for different variables: the obstacle function, value function, and population density can be represented in separate feature spaces, accommodating obstacles that are substantially less regular than the corresponding PDE solutions. Moreover, boundary conditions can be enforced through collocation on irregular domains without constructing boundary-fitted meshes. Numerical experiments involving smooth and discontinuous obstacles, a domain with holes, and higher-dimensional problems demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.

papers.title: A Monotone Meshfree-Particle Method for Mean Field Games on Scattered Point Clouds
papers.abstract: We develop a monotone meshfree--particle method for mean field games (MFGs). We discretize the backward Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation on a fixed scattered cloud, transport the forward Fokker--Planck law with reflected and killed particles, and close the fictitious-play loop by interpolation and mass-preserving kernel density estimation. Monotonicity is imposed row by row on two-dimensional clouds. Each row combines a positive generalized finite difference Laplacian with a nonnegative decomposition of the drift along rays to surrounding visible neighbors, with mirror images at reflecting walls, and every fixed-policy matrix is an M-matrix for arbitrary cell-P\'eclet number. We prove a discrete comparison principle and, on polygons with re-entrant corners included, that one HJB solve at a prescribed density converges to the viscosity solution off the boundary vertices, for convex Hamiltonians of at most quadratic growth under a structure condition. On a two-room floor plan with re-entrant door jambs, the computed HJB solutions converge to exact ones. A source-free exact MFG tests the fully coupled computation. At matched degrees of freedom on a grid domain, the meshfree HJB solve has a larger $L^2$ error and a smaller $L^\infty$ error than a five-point finite-difference solve, and is about twice as expensive including the stencil construction. On a non-convex evacuation game, the interior nodes of nine clouds receive monotone rows, apart from a few next to the boundary vertices that copy a neighbor.

papers.title: Learning Rate Transfer and Feature Learning Across Depth for Constrained Spectral Optimizers: Complete Scion
papers.abstract: Hyperparameter transfer across model depth is instrumental in training deep models, as it enables learning rates calibrated on shallow networks to be effectively applied to deeper architectures. The recent CompleteP framework establishes a $1/L$ residual scaling rule that demonstrates this for Adam-family optimizers. We study whether similar transfer extends to constrained optimization methods, specifically Frank-Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent, where updates are determined by linear minimization oracles. We derive scaling rules for these methods which confirm that the $1/L$ residual scaling applies, although the arguments differ from the Adam-family optimizers. Our analysis supports depth-wise transfer and width-wise transfer of the learning rate for the Scion algorithm while ensuring feature learning and avoiding the kernel-regime. In experiments on NLP transformers (nanoGPT on FineWeb), vision transformers (DeiT on ImageNet), and vision MLPs (MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10), we observe learning rate transfer across depth and feature learning for appropriately chosen residual scaling.

papers.title: Matrix-Based Ant Colony Search with Batched Decoding for Hierarchical Replenishment Routing: A Stylized Case Study Based on Korean City Data
papers.abstract: We study a stylized single-vehicle replenishment-routing problem in which the cities of a national logistics network are both demand points and supply points: a vehicle of limited capacity delivers to every city once, and when its load is insufficient for the next city it must detour to a city already served that can still supply goods. A 100-node benchmark is built from Korean population and geographic data, with the cities divided into 10 levels; the per-visit supply coefficient and the allowed number of stops decrease geometrically with the level. Building on matrix-based ant colony optimization, we keep the states of the whole colony in arrays, couple route construction with a fixed greedy replenishment-decoding policy, and evaluate the candidate moves of a local search in batches. With frozen parameters and 30 runs on seeds never used for tuning, the matrix-based ant colony search with the batch local search (MACO) reaches a mean total distance of 3081.7 km; a genetic algorithm equipped with the same local search at the same frequency reaches 3074.9 km (no significant difference), and a MAX-MIN ant system with the same local search 3142.2 km. Ablation identifies the batch local search as the main contributor to solution quality; a load-aware transition factor gives no significant gain. Within the parameter ranges tested, raising the supply coefficients of the cities below the top level shortens the route more than relaxing the stop limits, which are not binding here.

papers.title: Finite Element Approximation of Three-Dimensional Elliptic Optimal Control Problems with Curve-Supported Controls
papers.abstract: We consider a linear-quadratic elliptic optimal control problem in three dimensions with a box-constrained control supported on a compact embedded $C^{1,1}$ curve strictly contained in a bounded convex polyhedral domain. The right-hand side of the state equation is a measure supported on the curve, and the state is singular along it. We establish well-posedness and first-order optimality conditions and derive curve-adapted weighted inequalities and finite element error estimates for the singular state. For continuous piecewise linear finite elements on quasi-uniform tetrahedral meshes and variational discretization of the control, assuming exact integration over the curve, we prove the almost quadratic estimate $\|\bar q-\bar q_h\|_{L^2(\gamma)}\le Ch^2(1+\abs{\ln h})^3$. The proof of this estimate requires new results, which are of independent interest. The convergence rate observed in a numerical experiment is consistent with the predicted algebraic order.

papers.title: Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation: Estimating Peaks From the Contour Lines of Evaluated Solutions
papers.abstract: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) evaluate many candidate solutions but use them mainly to rank individuals. This paper treats the evaluated solutions as the spot heights of a topographic survey and draws the contour lines they imply. The contour map decomposes the evaluated region into peaks: in two dimensions a contour tree with persistence separates significant peaks from interpolation ripples, and in more dimensions hill climbing on the interpolated surface locates the peaks and ray-cast level sets describe them. A memory of the explored peaks directs the search to new ones. The data-supported contours of each peak are extrapolated to zero size by an area law, exact for quadratic peaks and second-order accurate for smooth ones, that estimates a peak's location, height and shape before it is sampled. A contour-assisted EA (CA-EA) inserts contour steps with local search and peak memory into a genetic algorithm (GA), differential evolution or particle swarm optimization. A contour-assisted surrogate-assisted EA (CA-SAEA), for expensive problems, spends each evaluation on surrogate-screened offspring or on sampling around a peak, entered at the maximum of the interpolated surface. On 2-D benchmarks, CA-EA reduces the evaluations a plain GA needs by factors of 12 to 112; controls attribute its gain over classical memetic search to restarting local search on distinct peaks. On the CEC 2015 expensive suite in 10 and 30 dimensions, CA-SAEA has the second-best average rank, behind DYCORS and ahead of lq-CMA-ES and the competition winner MVMO, although in 30 dimensions MVMO wins significantly on 9 functions and loses on 6; there the map beats sampling around the best point on 5 of 15 functions and loses on 3. Entering the peaks at their extrapolated locations brought no gain at these budgets, although, with enough samples, it improves the estimated heights on most two-dimensional functions.

papers.title: Quantifying the Cost of Restoring AC Feasibility for Approximate Optimal Power Flow Solutions
